summary: Agent Pay runs on card rails, so card law and network rules apply: Regulation Z and E in the US, PSD2 consent and SCA in the EU, the UK Payment Services Regulations, and Mastercard's own rules. No regulator had published agent-specific liability rules as of 2026-10-21. The Mastercard Rules (2026-06-02 edition) add no agent-specific liability rule, but they require pass-through wallet operators and checkout facilitators in Agent Pay to follow the Mastercard Agent Pay Program Standards, which are not public. Visa's rules, which govern Visa and its member institutions and yield to applicable law, make the cardholder responsible, within Visa's system, for an Agentic Payment Provider's actions. Visa calls none of its agent rules a liability shift, and Worldpay (2026-07-30) says none exists yet; issuers and acquirers keep existing card liability until that changes.

rows.text: Regulation Z caps cardholder liability for unauthorized credit card use; whether an agent acting outside its limits has apparent authority is an open question.

For debit cards, Regulation E excludes transfers by a person the consumer gave the access device to, unless the consumer has notified the financial institution that such transfers are no longer authorized. A consumer who authorizes an agent on a debit card may therefore carry the agent's transfers until the institution is notified.
Senator Warner asked Treasury on 2026-06-02 to examine how current law allocates liability when agents err; no rule followed yet.

California's ADMT regulations took effect on 2026-01-01; a business already using ADMT for significant decisions must comply by 2027-01-01. They cover only significant decisions: providing or denying financial or lending services, housing, education, employment or healthcare. An agent platform that chooses purchases, or a merchant that accepts agent orders, is generally not making such a decision.

The RTS on SCA require dynamic linking of amount and payee for remote payments. Verifiable Intent presents its constraints and checkout_hash as a cryptographic form of dynamic linking but says it does not replace SCA.

PSD2 treats a payment as authorized only with the payer's consent, which can be given in advance and for a series of transactions in the form agreed with the payment service provider (Article 64), and caps payer liability for unauthorized ones. Whether a Verifiable Intent Autonomous mandate counts as that agreed form of consent is untested.

AI Act Article 50(1) applies from 2026-08-02: providers of AI systems meant to interact directly with people must design them so people know they deal with an AI, unless that is obvious. Generative systems on the market before that date have until 2026-12-02 for the Article 50(2) marking duty.
GDPR applies to the consumer data in mastercardIdToken and Verifiable Intent claims; Verifiable Intent keeps sub and pan_last_four always visible.
The Payment Services Regulations 2017 treat a transaction as authorized only with payer consent (regulation 67) and cap payer liability at GBP 35 with exceptions (regulation 77).
HM Treasury consulted from 2026-07-14 to 2026-10-06 on how authentication, consent and liability should adapt for agentic payments; no response yet.
The FCA said on 2026-03-25 it will consider with HM Treasury whether regulation must change for agentic payments.

The Retail Payment Activities Act has required payment service providers to have risk management and safeguarding frameworks since 2025-09-08. No agent-specific liability rule was found on the Bank of Canada's retail payments supervision page (read 2026-10-20).

PIPEDA governs personal information, such as the consumer data in mastercardIdToken and Verifiable Intent claims, that agent platforms and merchants collect, use or disclose in the course of commercial activities. Collection, use and disclosure within Quebec, Alberta or British Columbia falls under provincial law instead, except at federally regulated businesses (exemption orders under section 26(2)(b)).
MAS Guidelines on AI Risk Management (issued 2026-10-07, effective 2027-10-07) name agentic AI systems and apply to issuers in Singapore.

MAS's E-Payments User Protection Guidelines set liability for unauthorized transactions and duties for erroneous ones on protected accounts. Their liability apportionment does not apply to credit, charge or debit cards issued in Singapore, which follow the ABS Code of Practice for Banks. The Guidelines do not address agents.

Mastercard says standard chargeback rights apply to agentic transactions. The 2026-06-02 Mastercard Rules add no agent-specific liability rule. They require pass-through wallet operators and checkout facilitators in Agent Pay to follow the Mastercard Agent Pay Program Standards. A web search on 2026-10-19 found no public copy of those standards, and Worldpay (2026-07-30) says no liability shift exists yet.
EMVCo's draft agentic framework (2026-09-01) proposes Intent Services that would complement Verifiable Intent and lists Know Your Agent and agent transaction indicators as possible future work.
Mastercard says merchants accepting agent tokens keep their PCI scope unchanged, because they receive tokens, not card numbers.
